cards.title: What a Model Registry Is
cards.teaser: A model registry is the system-of-record for trained models — a versioned, governed store that tracks not just the model artifact but its lineage, lifecycle stage, approvals, and deployment history.

runs.text: In software engineering, an artifact registry (Docker Hub, Nexus, Artifactory) stores versioned build outputs and enforces promotion policies before those outputs reach production. A
model registry
plays the same role for ML: it is the authoritative store of trained models, providing versioning, metadata, lineage tracking, lifecycle management, and access control in one place.

Without a registry, organizations fall into what practitioners call the "model spreadsheet" anti-pattern: a shared document listing model filenames, S3 paths, and Slack threads where someone explained which version is in production. That information is stale within days. When a production incident requires an emergency rollback, nobody can confidently answer which file to restore.
A model registry solves four problems simultaneously:

items.text: Discovery
— any team member can find which model is in production for a given use case, what version it is, and when it was promoted.
Governance
— promotion between lifecycle stages (development to staging to production) requires explicit approval, creating an audit trail.
Reproducibility
— every registered model version links back to the training run, dataset version, and code commit that produced it.
Deployment source
— serving infrastructure pulls models from the registry by name and stage, decoupling deployment from the training pipeline.

runs.text: The MLflow Model Registry (2019), Amazon SageMaker Model Registry, Google Vertex AI Model Registry, and Azure ML Model Registry all implement this pattern with varying levels of managed infrastructure. The conceptual model is consistent across all of them.

A model registry is the single source of truth for trained models — it records what exists, which version is in production, who approved it, and where it came from. Without one, that knowledge lives in spreadsheets and Slack threads that go stale immediately.

cards.title: Model Versioning
cards.teaser: Every model registered in a registry gets a version — an immutable identifier that ties the artifact to the exact training run, dataset snapshot, code commit, and hyperparameters that produced it.

runs.text: Model versioning is not the same as software semantic versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH), though some teams adopt that notation for registered models. A model version must capture more than a human-readable label — it must be traceable to its full provenance.
A complete model version identifier typically includes:

items.text: Version number
— an auto-incrementing integer assigned by the registry (MLflow uses integers: 1, 2, 3). Some teams layer semantic version tags on top.
Run ID
— the experiment tracking run that produced this model. Links to logged metrics, parameters, and artifacts.
Artifact hash
— a SHA-256 digest of the serialized model file(s). Proves the artifact has not been modified after registration.
Timestamp
— the time the model was registered, not when training completed (which may differ for batch training jobs).
Source URI
— the artifact store path where the serialized model files reside (e.g., an S3 path or GCS bucket).

runs.text: Model versions are
immutable

once registered. Retraining with new data produces a new version, not an overwrite of the existing one. This immutability is what makes rollback reliable: rolling back means pointing production at a prior version number, not reconstructing a past state.

Overwriting a model artifact at a versioned path is a registry integrity violation. Serving systems cache artifact paths; an overwrite creates a silent inconsistency between what the registry records and what is actually deployed. Registries enforce immutability to prevent this.

A model version is an immutable record: this exact artifact, produced by this exact training run, at this timestamp. You can add new versions but you cannot edit old ones — that immutability is what makes rollbacks trustworthy.

cards.title: Lifecycle Stages
cards.teaser: MLflow's four lifecycle stages — None, Staging, Production, Archived — define the progression of a model from experimental artifact to deployed system to retired record. The stage is the registry's answer to "is this model safe to serve?"

runs.text: MLflow introduced the canonical lifecycle stage vocabulary that most registries have adopted in some form. Each stage communicates a different level of validation and operational intent:

items.text: None
— the default stage when a model is first registered. The model exists in the registry but has not been reviewed or tested for deployment. This is the intake stage.
Staging

— the model is under evaluation. Integration tests, A/B shadow traffic, load tests, fairness audits, and stakeholder reviews happen here. A model in Staging is a candidate for production, not a commitment.
Production

— the model has passed all gates and is approved to serve live traffic. Serving infrastructure is pointed at models in this stage. Typically only one model version per use case is in Production at any given time (though champion/challenger patterns may temporarily hold two).
Archived

— the model has been superseded or retired. Archived models are retained for audit and reproducibility but are not deployed. Transitioning to Archived is reversible in principle but requires explicit re-promotion through the full approval workflow.

runs.text: These stages are not just labels — they are gates. Serving systems, access control policies, and monitoring configurations all filter by stage. A model in "None" should never be reachable by production serving infrastructure; a model in "Archived" should trigger alerts if any serving system attempts to load it.

Some organizations extend the standard four stages. Common additions include "Champion" and "Challenger" sub-stages within Production for A/B testing, and a "Deprecated" stage before Archived that signals "stop routing traffic to this" without full archival. The core vocabulary remains None / Staging / Production / Archived.

Lifecycle stages are the registry's way of saying "how vetted is this model?" None means untested, Staging means under evaluation, Production means approved and live, and Archived means retired but kept for records.

cards.title: Stage Transitions and Approval Gates
cards.teaser: Moving a model between lifecycle stages is a deliberate act, not an automatic one. Approval gates encode the organization's quality bar — the questions that must be answered before a model can serve production traffic.

runs.text: In a CI/CD pipeline, a deployment gate might require: tests pass, security scan is clean, a senior engineer approves. A model registry uses the same pattern but the gate criteria are domain-specific to ML.
A typical
None → Staging
gate checks:

items.text: Model artifact is loadable and passes schema validation (expected input/output signatures).
Offline evaluation metrics meet the minimum threshold (e.g., F1 > 0.85 on the held-out test set).
Model card is complete and has been reviewed.

runs.text: A
Staging → Production
gate is stricter:

items.text: Shadow or canary traffic results confirm the model performs no worse than the current production model on live data.
Latency and resource consumption are within SLA bounds under realistic load.
Fairness and bias evaluation has been completed and documented.
A named approver (often the ML lead, a product stakeholder, or both) has signed off in the registry UI.

runs.text: Stage transitions should be
logged immutably
: who initiated the transition, at what time, with what justification. This log is the model's audit trail and is often required for regulatory compliance (GDPR, EU AI Act, financial regulations).

Approval gates that can be bypassed under "emergency" conditions provide a false sense of governance. Every bypass should be logged with a mandatory justification, and bypass rates should be reviewed in post-incident analysis.

A stage transition is a gate: to move a model from Staging to Production, you must answer a specific set of questions (does it meet quality thresholds? has someone approved it?) and the answers are recorded permanently.

cards.title: Model Cards
cards.teaser: A model card is a short document attached to every registered model — it describes what the model does, who should use it, what data it was trained on, and where it fails. Mitchell et al. introduced the framework at Google in 2019.

runs.text: Margaret Mitchell, Timnit Gebru, and colleagues at Google published "Model Cards for Model Reporting" (FAccT 2019), introducing a standardized framework for documenting machine learning models. The paper argued that model artifacts shipped without documentation create liability — developers integrating the model have no way to assess whether it is appropriate for their use case.
A model card contains eight sections:

items.text: Model details
— name, version, type (classifier, regressor, embedding model), framework, and the team that developed it.
Intended use
— primary use cases the model was designed for; explicitly out-of-scope uses the model should not be applied to.
Factors
— relevant demographic, environmental, or technical factors (e.g., language, age group, device type) that influence model behavior.
Metrics
— performance metrics and their values on evaluation datasets. Both overall performance and performance disaggregated by relevant subgroups.
Evaluation data
— what datasets were used to evaluate the model, how they were collected, and their known limitations.
Training data
— datasets used for training and their provenance (respecting data licensing and privacy constraints).
Quantitative analyses
— performance broken down by relevant subgroups, ideally as charts or tables showing where the model underperforms.
Ethical considerations and caveats
— known failure modes, bias risks, and guidance for ethical deployment.

runs.text: In a model registry, a model card is attached to each registered model and must be complete before a model can advance from Staging to Production. The card is a living document: it is updated as new evaluations are completed or new use cases are discovered.

Mitchell et al.'s original paper is available at arxiv.org/abs/1810.03993. The framework has been adopted by Hugging Face (model cards on the Hub), Google (Responsible AI practices), and the EU AI Act's documentation requirements all trace to the same conceptual foundation.

A model card is the instruction manual for a model — it tells you what the model was built to do, what data trained it, how well it performs on different groups, and where it breaks down. Without one, integrators are flying blind.

cards.title: Model Lineage
cards.teaser: Model lineage traces the complete provenance of a registered model — the training run, the dataset version, the feature pipeline, and the code commit that produced it. Lineage turns a model artifact into an auditable result.

runs.text: A model is not just a file — it is the output of a chain of decisions and data. Lineage captures that chain so that, given any registered model version, you can answer:

items.text: Which training code version produced this model?
Which dataset version (or dataset snapshot) was used?
Which feature pipeline produced the features the model consumed?
What hyperparameters were used?
What were the training environment details (Python version, framework version, hardware)?

runs.text: Lineage is particularly critical for incident response. When a model behaves unexpectedly in production — predicting wrong labels, exhibiting bias on a newly observed segment, or degrading suddenly — lineage tells you where to look. If the dataset changed between version 4 and version 5, that is where the investigation starts.

Lineage is also the bridge between the experiment tracking system and the model registry. When a training run is logged in MLflow Tracking or Weights & Biases, and the resulting model is registered, the registry stores a pointer back to that run ID. From the run, you can trace back to the dataset version logged as an input artifact.

In practice, complete lineage requires all upstream systems to participate: the data versioning system (DVC, Delta Lake snapshots) must log versioned dataset identifiers, the feature store must record feature pipeline versions, and the training job must log all of these as run inputs.

Lineage means you can point at any model version and trace backwards to the exact data, code, and configuration that produced it. That traceability is what makes incident investigations possible and regulatory audits feasible.

cards.title: Aliases and Tags
cards.teaser: Aliases are semantic pointers to specific model versions — "production", "champion", "challenger". Tags are free-form key-value metadata. Together they let serving systems and humans refer to models by role rather than by version number.

runs.text: Version numbers are opaque to serving systems. A model server configured to load "fraud-detection, version 47" must be reconfigured every time a new model version is promoted to production. Aliases solve this by providing a stable, semantic pointer that can be redirected without changing the serving infrastructure.
Common alias patterns:

items.text: production

— the currently deployed model. Serving systems load the version this alias points to. When version 48 is promoted, the alias is updated; serving infrastructure picks up the change at next load without a config change.
champion
— the current best-performing model in production. Equivalent to
production
in most setups; the distinction matters when multiple models serve the same endpoint.
challenger
— a candidate model receiving a fraction of live traffic in an A/B experiment. When the challenger wins, it becomes the new champion.
baseline
— the reference model for evaluating new candidates, often a simple rule-based or sklearn model.

runs.text: Tags are key-value pairs attached to a model version. Examples:

items.text: validated_by: alice@company.com
approved_for: eu_traffic
bias_audit: passed_2024_q2
do_not_delete: true

runs.text: Tags are searchable: a compliance team can query the registry for all models without a completed bias audit tag and prioritize them for review. Unlike aliases, tags can coexist — a version can have multiple tags but at most one assignment per alias name.

An alias is a named pointer like a DNS entry — "production" points to version 47 today and version 48 tomorrow, and the serving system doesn't need to know which number. A tag is a sticky label you attach for search and governance purposes.

cards.title: The Registry as Deployment Source
cards.teaser: Production serving systems pull models from the registry by name and alias — not by file path, S3 key, or Slack link. The registry is the only authorized source of truth for what model is running in production.

runs.text: The registry-as-deployment-source pattern decouples training from deployment. The training pipeline writes models
into
the registry; serving infrastructure reads models
from
the registry. Neither side needs to know about the other's implementation.
A serving system configured to load by alias looks like this conceptually:

items.text: On startup, the model server calls the registry API: "give me the model artifact for use case 'fraud-detection' with alias 'production'."
The registry resolves the alias to a version number, retrieves the artifact store URI, and returns it.
The model server downloads the artifact and loads it into memory.
On a configurable polling interval (or via a webhook), the server checks if the 'production' alias now points to a different version. If so, it hot-reloads.

runs.text: This pattern enforces governance by construction: serving infrastructure
cannot

load a model that has not gone through the registry's approval workflow, because it only knows how to talk to the registry. Ad-hoc deployments of model files copied from a training machine are architecturally impossible.

MLflow's model serving command (mlflow models serve) loads by registered model name and stage. SageMaker Inference Endpoints load from the Model Registry. Vertex AI Prediction loads from the Vertex AI Model Registry. In all cases the serving layer is decoupled from the training layer by the registry interface.
When serving infrastructure only knows how to load models from the registry, governance is enforced automatically — a model that hasn't been approved and registered simply cannot be deployed.

cards.title: Promotion Workflows
cards.teaser: A promotion workflow is an automated pipeline that gates a model's advance from one lifecycle stage to the next — running integration tests, performance benchmarks, shadow traffic, and bias checks before a human approval step.

runs.text: Promotion workflows apply CI/CD thinking to the model lifecycle. Just as software CI runs tests before merging to main, a model promotion workflow runs model-specific checks before updating the registry alias that production serving infrastructure consults.
A typical
Staging → Production
promotion workflow:

items.text: Trigger
: A new model version is transitioned to Staging in the registry (manually or by the training pipeline).
Schema validation
: Confirm the model's input/output signature matches the serving contract. Fail fast if the API contract has changed without a corresponding serving update.
Offline evaluation
: Run the evaluation suite on the held-out test set and compare metrics to the current production model. Block promotion if the challenger underperforms.
Load and latency testing
: Serve the model under simulated production load. Verify p95 and p99 latency are within SLA.
Shadow traffic
(optional): Route a copy of live traffic to the challenger while production traffic continues to go to the champion. Compare prediction distributions for unexpected divergence.
Human approval
: A notification is sent to the model owner and approver with a summary of all automated check results. The approver reviews and approves (or rejects) in the registry UI.
Alias update
: On approval, the workflow automatically updates the 'production' alias to point to the new version. Serving infrastructure picks up the change.

runs.text: Automated tests that only compare aggregate metrics (overall accuracy) can miss regressions on specific subgroups. Production models for sensitive use cases should include disaggregated evaluation as a required gate, not an optional one.

A promotion workflow is the automated checklist a model must pass before it can go to production — schema check, performance comparison, load test, bias audit, then a human approval. It prevents a bad model from reaching users through human error or time pressure.

cards.title: Audit Trail
cards.teaser: Every stage transition, alias update, approval, and rejection in the registry is logged immutably — who did what, when, and why. The audit trail is what transforms a model registry from a file store into a governance system.

runs.text: Regulatory frameworks increasingly require organizations to document the decision process for deployed AI systems. The EU AI Act (2024), financial services regulations (SR 11-7 model risk management guidance), and healthcare AI guidelines all require an audit trail that answers: who authorized this model to make decisions about people, and on what basis?
A complete audit trail in a model registry records:

items.text: Registration events
: who registered the model version, from which training run, at what time.
Stage transition events
: who requested the transition, who approved it, and any written justification.
Rejection events
: who rejected a promotion request and the stated reason. Rejections are as important as approvals for understanding the decision process.
Alias update events
: when the 'production' alias was pointed at a new version and by whom.
Emergency bypass events
: any promotion that skipped a required gate, with mandatory justification.
Model card update events
: who changed the card content and when.

runs.text: Audit trail entries should be
append-only
and
non-repudiable

: no one — including registry administrators — should be able to delete or modify a historical entry. Some organizations store audit trail entries in a separate append-only log (an immutable S3 bucket, a WORM storage tier, or an audit log service) rather than the registry database, specifically to meet regulatory immutability requirements.

The audit trail is the permanent record of every decision made about a model — who promoted it, who rejected it, who approved the emergency bypass. Without it, a post-incident review or a regulatory audit cannot reconstruct what happened or why.

cards.title: MLflow Model Registry in Practice
cards.teaser: MLflow's Model Registry is the open-source standard — it adds versioning, lifecycle stages, and approval workflows on top of MLflow Tracking's experiment and artifact stores. A single mlflow.register_model() call is all it takes to start.

runs.text: MLflow Model Registry (introduced in MLflow 1.0) is the most widely used open-source registry implementation. It integrates directly with MLflow Tracking: a logged model artifact can be registered in one call and immediately participates in the full lifecycle workflow.
A minimal end-to-end example:

explanation.text:
import mlflow
import mlflow.sklearn
from mlflow import MlflowClient
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier

# 1. Train and log the model
mlflow.set_experiment("fraud-detection")

with mlflow.start_run() as run:
    clf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100, max_depth=6)
    clf.fit(X_train, y_train)

    mlflow.log_param("n_estimators", 100)
    mlflow.log_param("max_depth", 6)
    mlflow.log_metric("f1_score", f1)
    mlflow.log_metric("roc_auc", roc_auc)

    # Log with an MLflow Model signature
    signature = mlflow.models.infer_signature(X_train, clf.predict(X_train))
    mlflow.sklearn.log_model(
        clf,
        artifact_path="model",
        signature=signature,
        registered_model_name="fraud-detection"  # auto-registers on log
    )

# 2. Transition to Staging
client = MlflowClient()
client.transition_model_version_stage(
    name="fraud-detection",
    version=1,
    stage="Staging",
    archive_existing_versions=False
)

# 3. After evaluation, transition to Production
client.transition_model_version_stage(
    name="fraud-detection",
    version=1,
    stage="Production",
    archive_existing_versions=True  # archives current Production version
)

# 4. Load from registry by stage (serving side)
model = mlflow.sklearn.load_model("models:/fraud-detection/Production")
predictions = model.predict(X_serve)

# 5. Set an alias (MLflow 2.x)
client.set_registered_model_alias(
    name="fraud-detection",
    alias="champion",
    version="1"
)
# Load by alias
model = mlflow.sklearn.load_model("models:/fraud-detection@champion")

runs.text: The URI scheme
models:/fraud-detection/Production

is the stable pointer serving infrastructure uses. When version 2 is promoted to Production (and version 1 is archived), loading this URI automatically returns version 2 — no serving configuration change required.

MLflow 2.x deprecated stage-based transitions in favor of aliases for new workflows. The stage model (None/Staging/Production/Archived) remains supported but aliases (e.g., @champion, @production) are the preferred forward-looking pattern. Both are available in current MLflow releases.

With MLflow, you register a model by adding registered_model_name to your log_model call. After that, one API call transitions it to Staging, another to Production. The serving side just loads models:/model-name/Production and gets whatever version is currently there.

cards.title: Managed Registries: SageMaker, Vertex AI, Azure ML
cards.teaser: AWS, Google, and Azure all provide managed model registries deeply integrated with their ML platforms. They offer the same lifecycle semantics as MLflow but add cloud-native IAM, automated approval workflows, and direct integration with their serving infrastructure.

runs.text: Each major cloud provider's managed registry maps to the same conceptual model but with platform-specific implementation:

items.text: Amazon SageMaker Model Registry

— models are stored in Model Package Groups with versioned Model Packages. Lifecycle stages are modeled as approval statuses: PendingManualApproval, Approved, Rejected. Approved models can be automatically deployed to SageMaker Endpoints via CI/CD pipelines built with SageMaker Pipelines or CodePipeline.
Google Vertex AI Model Registry

— integrated with Vertex AI Experiments and Vertex AI Pipelines. Models are stored as Vertex AI Model resources with versioned model artifacts. Promotion to Vertex AI Endpoints is managed through the registry. Supports model evaluation reports attached to each version.
Azure Machine Learning Model Registry

— part of the AzureML workspace. Models are registered with the AzureML SDK or CLI and assigned lifecycle stages (Development, Production, Archived). Integration with Azure DevOps or GitHub Actions allows automated promotion workflows triggered by pipeline events.

runs.text: Managed registries provide advantages over self-hosted MLflow:

items.text: IAM integration
: registry access is controlled by the cloud provider's identity system (AWS IAM, GCP IAM, Azure RBAC), not a separate credential store.
Artifact storage managed
: model artifacts are stored in the provider's native object storage with automatic lifecycle policies and server-side encryption.
Native serving integration
: deploying a registered model to a managed endpoint is a single SDK call or console click.

runs.text: The trade-off is vendor lock-in. Organizations that use SageMaker's registry are coupled to SageMaker's serving infrastructure. Teams that need multi-cloud or on-premises flexibility often choose self-hosted MLflow or Weights & Biases, accepting the additional operational overhead.

SageMaker, Vertex AI, and Azure ML each offer a managed registry with the same lifecycle semantics as MLflow but tightly integrated with their cloud's identity, storage, and serving services. The benefit is less infrastructure to operate; the cost is tighter coupling to one cloud vendor.

cards.title: Model Registry vs Artifact Store
cards.teaser: An artifact store holds binary blobs. A model registry holds governed model versions with lifecycle stages, lineage, approval workflows, and audit trails. The registry uses an artifact store as its backend — they are complementary, not interchangeable.

runs.text: This confusion is one of the most common in MLOps architecture discussions. Both an artifact store (S3, GCS, Azure Blob Storage, or MLflow's local artifact directory) and a model registry store model files. The difference is everything that surrounds the file.

items.text: Artifact store

— stores binary files at addressable paths. Has no concept of versioning beyond file naming conventions (if any). Has no lifecycle stages. Has no approval workflows. Has no lineage tracking. An S3 bucket is an artifact store.
Model registry

— stores versioned model records that point to artifact locations. Adds lifecycle stages (None/Staging/Production/Archived). Adds approval workflows and an audit trail. Adds lineage linking each version to its training run and dataset. Adds aliases for semantic addressing.

runs.text: A model registry always has an artifact store as its backend. In MLflow, the artifact store (configured as S3, GCS, or a local path) holds the actual model files; the registry database (SQLite or a production database) holds the metadata, versions, stages, and audit logs. When you call
mlflow.sklearn.load_model("models:/fraud-detection/Production")
, the registry resolves the stage to a version number, looks up the artifact store path for that version, and returns the model from storage.
The practical implication: a team that only uses an artifact store (uploading serialized models to S3 with a naming convention like
models/fraud/v47/model.pkl
) has built a filesystem-based "registry" with none of the governance properties. They have artifact storage but no governance. The registry adds the governance layer on top.

"We store models in S3" is not a model registry. It is a file store with manual conventions. As the model count grows, those conventions decay: version numbering becomes inconsistent, lineage is lost, and the answer to "what is in production?" requires reading a deploy script.

An artifact store is where the model bytes live. The registry is the card catalog on top — it tracks versions, stages, who approved what, and which run produced each version. Every registry has an artifact store as its backend; not every artifact store has a registry in front of it.

cards.title: Model Card Structure in Practice
cards.teaser: A model card is most useful when it is machine-readable, stored alongside the model in the registry, and automatically populated from training metadata — reducing documentation burden while increasing completeness.

runs.text: The original Model Cards paper (Mitchell et al., 2019) describes eight sections as a conceptual framework. In practice, teams implement model cards as structured YAML or JSON files that are logged as artifacts alongside the model and rendered by the registry UI.
A minimal machine-readable model card:

explanation.text:
model_card:
  model_details:
    name: fraud-detection
    version: "3"
    type: binary_classifier
    framework: scikit-learn 1.4
    team: payments-ml
    contact: payments-ml@company.com
    license: proprietary

  intended_use:
    primary_uses:
      - "Flag card-not-present transactions for manual review"
    out_of_scope_uses:
      - "Automated transaction blocking without human review"
      - "Identity verification"

  training_data:
    dataset: transactions-v12
    version_hash: sha256:a3f9b1...
    date_range: "2022-01-01 to 2024-06-30"
    size: 48_000_000
    exclusions: "Transactions under $1 excluded"

  evaluation_data:
    dataset: transactions-test-v12
    size: 4_800_000
    temporal_split: "2024-07-01 to 2024-09-30"

  metrics:
    overall:
      f1: 0.891
      precision: 0.903
      recall: 0.879
      roc_auc: 0.961
    by_transaction_amount:
      under_100:
        f1: 0.842
      100_to_1000:
        f1: 0.901
      over_1000:
        f1: 0.921

  ethical_considerations:
    known_limitations:
      - "Performance degrades on new merchant categories not present in training data"
      - "Higher false positive rate on first-time cardholders"
    bias_evaluation: "bias-audit-2024-q3"
    fairness_constraints: none_applied

  caveats:
    - "Do not deploy in jurisdictions requiring explainability without adding a SHAP layer"
    - "Retrain if transaction volume distribution shifts by more than 15% (drift threshold)"

runs.text: Many fields in a model card can be auto-populated from the experiment tracking system: metrics come from logged run results, dataset hash comes from the data versioning system, framework version from the logged environment. The sections requiring human input — intended use, ethical considerations, caveats — are where the team adds judgment.

A well-implemented model card is mostly auto-filled from training metadata — the metrics, the dataset version, the framework. The parts a human must write are the ones that require judgment: what is this model for, what should it never be used for, and where does it underperform.

cards.title: Registry Design Patterns and Pitfalls
cards.teaser: A registry that everyone can write to but nobody owns becomes a dumping ground. Effective registries enforce naming conventions, require model cards before Staging, and run regular archival sweeps to keep the active model set legible.

runs.text: A model registry, like any shared system, requires governance policies to remain useful at scale. Teams that deploy a registry without accompanying policies consistently encounter the same failure modes:

items.text: The graveyard registry.

Hundreds of model versions registered in the "None" stage that nobody owns, from experiments that ended months ago. The registry becomes noise. Mitigation: automated archival of versions that have been in "None" for more than 30 days without any tag or activity.
The naming convention collapse.

Models are registered as "model-v2", "model-final", "model-FINAL-v2", "model-prod". Serving infrastructure cannot reliably construct a registry path. Mitigation: enforce a registry naming policy (e.g.,
{domain}-{use-case}
) and reject registrations that don't match.
The phantom production model.

A model is deployed by copying a file directly to the serving host, bypassing the registry. The registry says version 12 is in production; the actual deployed model is a file with no registry entry. Mitigation: serving infrastructure must not accept model files from any source other than the registry API.
The approval rubber stamp.

Approvers approve promotions without reviewing evaluation results because the approval UI shows no context. Mitigation: the approval workflow must surface the comparison between the candidate and the current production model in the approval notification.

runs.text: The most effective registries treat themselves as products with internal users. They have an owner (usually a platform or MLOps team), documented policies, and a regular review process for the naming conventions and governance gates. Without ownership, entropy wins.

Apply the same "definition of done" discipline from CI/CD to the registry. For each lifecycle stage boundary, write down the specific conditions that must be true. Post that list in the registry documentation. Conditions that are not written down are not enforced.

A registry without governance policies is just a cluttered file store with extra steps. The pitfalls are predictable — too many stale versions, inconsistent naming, approval shortcuts. Each one has a specific fix, but they all require someone to own the registry as a product.
